text: [excited] This is Max. At nine a.m. today, Max blinked… and saw ten a.m. [tense] He's in a hot-air balloon. Out of control. Over the city. Holding the dog. And underneath him… fireworks. [whisper] Then future Max turns, looks straight at him, and screams two words. "DON'T GO!" [urgent] The vision ends. Max has sixty minutes to stop it. [sarcastic] I'd tell you how it ends. But Max won't give me spoilers.

[playful] Nine-oh-two. Max tests it. He sees the bus will be late. He sees Mum will ask about his homework. He sees a pigeon in his future. Not a nice one. [excited] Then Max has a brilliant idea. The lottery. [deadpan] The draw is at eight p.m. His power sees one hour ahead. Of nine a.m. [sarcastic] Max, quick question. Do I get the promotion this year? Max? …He's ignoring me.

[curious] Here's the thing. You can already see the future. Just not very far. Light from the world takes time to get through your eyes and into your brain. By the time you see something, it's already about a tenth of a second old. So your brain cheats. It guesses where things will be and shows you the guess. It's how a tennis player returns a serve that reaches them in less than half a second. They're not reacting. They're predicting. [excited] So you've been seeing the future your whole life. About a tenth of a second of it. Max just got an upgrade. Thirty-six thousand times bigger. [tense] Nine-oh-eight. Max blinks again. And the vision is worse.

[tense] A festival. Thousands of people. A poster: "Fireworks, ten a.m. sharp." And the balloon… is shaped like a duck. [determined] Plan A. If Max never leaves the house, he can't end up in a duck. [deadpan] Nine-twelve. A sausage van drives past. Sir Biscuit has one thought. It's always the same thought. [urgent] He's through the dog flap. He's gone. Plan A lasted four minutes.

[building] So Max runs. Through the market. Past the bakery. Down the hill. [sarcastic] And here's the problem with Max's power. He can see exactly what happens in one hour. Which is no help at all when a fruit cart is coming at you in one second. He goes through a wedding cake. He borrows a skateboard. He does not give it back. [urgent] The van turns into the old town. So Max takes the shortcut. Across the rooftops. [building] Max has never done parkour. Jump one. Perfect. Jump two. Perfect. Jump three… [deadpan] …less perfect. [curious] Lying in the laundry, Max gets the weirdest feeling. Like he's been here before. Déjà vu. And that's real, but it's not the future. Some scientists think déjà vu is your brain's memory checker spotting a tiny mix-up, and flagging it. It's actually a sign your memory is working properly. [deadpan] Max's memory is working properly. His day is not. [tense] Nine-thirty. He blinks. Dave is in the basket too. Screaming. Because the balloon is a duck.

[determined] Plan B. Max phones Dave. "Dave, whatever happens, stay away from the festival." [deadpan] Dave has never once been told not to do something… without immediately doing it. [sarcastic] Great plan, Max. No notes. [curious] Every time Max changes something, the future changes too. And this is real. In 1961, a scientist called Edward Lorenz ran a weather simulation and typed 0.506 instead of 0.506127. A difference smaller than a crumb. [excited] His whole forecast came out completely different. Sunshine in one. Storms in the other. It's called the butterfly effect. Tiny change, massive future. It's why a ten-day weather forecast is barely better than a guess. [tense] Which means every orange Max knocked over… pushed him a little closer to that duck.

[determined] Plan C. No balloon, no problem. Max is going to pop the duck. [building] Nine-forty-eight. He sneaks into the festival. Past the hot dog stand. Under the stage. Right up to the duck. [tense] And a security guard sees him. [urgent] Max runs. Through the bouncy castle. Through the hall of mirrors, where there are suddenly twelve Maxes and the guard has no idea which one is real. [building] Through the dodgems. Over the dodgems. Into a giant fluffy cloud of candy floss. [deadpan] He escapes. He's sticky. And he's lost the pin. [tense] And when he looks up… he's right next to the balloon. Exactly where the vision said he'd be.

[building] Nine-fifty-five. And who's sitting in the basket? Sir Biscuit. Eating the sausage. Like he planned this. [urgent] Max jumps in to grab him. And who's been handed the rope? Dave. [deadpan] Dave looks up. Dave sees the duck. Dave lets go. [tense] Then he panics and jumps in after them. [whisper] Ten a.m. [building] And right on time… the fireworks.

[tense] Dave can't take it. He climbs onto the edge of the basket. He's going to jump. [urgent] And Max screams the two words he heard an hour ago. "DON'T GO!" [quiet] He was never warning himself. He was saving Dave. [warm] So Max does the one thing his power is actually good for. He blinks… and looks at eleven a.m. Then he tells Dave exactly what he sees. And this is real too. In one study, people were more stressed by a fifty-fifty chance of a small electric shock… than when they knew for certain it was coming. Not knowing is the scary part. [warm] So Max takes the not-knowing away. "In ten minutes, we land. In twenty, you're laughing. I've seen it." Dave climbs down.

[tense] Then the burner coughs. The flame shrinks. The fuel gauge drops into the red. [curious] Second problem. You can't steer a hot-air balloon. It just goes where the wind goes. But the wind blows different ways at different heights. [excited] So pilots go up and down to find a wind going the right way. Up. Wrong way. Down. Wrong way. Up a tiny bit… there. [building] They drift over the stadium in the middle of the big match. Sixty thousand people look up. And the duck lands… right on the centre spot. [warm] The festival gives Max free sausages for life. Sir Biscuit has never been happier. Dave kisses the grass.

[warm] Max learned two things today. You can't always stop the future. But you can make sure nobody faces it alone. [playful] If you could see one hour ahead, what would you use it for? Comments. [sarcastic] And Max, the promotion? Anything? …He says to watch out for pigeons at ten-oh-one.
